title: The tomb of Zeus in Crete
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα λέγει περὶ ἡμῶν ὅτι καταγελῶμεν τῶν προσκυνούντων τὸν Δία, ἐπεὶ τάφος αὐτοῦ ἐν Κρήτῃ δείκνυται, καὶ οὐδὲν ἧττον σέβομεν τὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ τάφου. οὐκ εἰδότες, πῶς καὶ καθὸ Κρῆτες τὸ τοιοῦτον ποιοῦσιν. ὅρα οὖν ὅτι ἐν τούτοις ἀπολογεῖται μὲν περὶ Κρητῶν καὶ τοῦ Διὸς καὶ τοῦ τάφου αὐτοῦ. αἰνιττόμενος τροπικὰς ὑπονοίας, καθ᾿ ἃς πεπλάσθαι λέγεται ὁ περὶ τοῦ Διὸς μῦθος· ἡμῶν δὲ κατηγορεῖ, ὁμολογούντων μὲν τετάφθαι τὸν ἡμέτερον Ἰησοῦν φασκόντων δὲ καὶ ἐγηγέρθαι αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ τάφου, ὅπερ Κρῆτες οὐκέτι περὶ τοῦ Διὸς ἱστοροῦσιν. ἐπεὶ δὲ δοκεῖ συναγορεύειν τῷ ἐν Κρήτῃ τάφῳ τοῦ Διὸς λέγων· ὅπως μὲν καὶ καθότι Κρῆτες τοῦτο ποιοῦσιν, οὐκ εἰδότες, φήσομεν ὅτι καὶ ὁ Κυρηναῖος Καλλίμαχος, πλεῖστα ὅσα ἀναγνοὺς ποιήματα καὶ ἱστορίαν σχεδὸν πᾶσαν ἀναλεξάμενος Ἑλληνικὴν, οὐδεμίαν οἶδε τροπολογίαν ἐν τοῖς περὶ Διὸς καὶ τοῦ τάφου αὐτοῦ. διὸ καὶ ἐγκαλεῖ τοῖς Κρησὶν ἐν τῷ εἰς τὸν Δία γραφέντι αὐτῷ ὕμνῳ λέγων· Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται· καὶ γὰρ τάφον, ὦ ἄνα. σεῖο Κρῆτες ἐτεκτήναντο· σὺ δ᾿ οὐ θάνες. ἐσσὶ γὰρ αἰεί. καὶ ὁ εἰπὼν „σὺ δ᾿ οὐ θάνες, ἐσσὶ γὰρ αἰεὶ.“ ἀρνησάμενος τὴν ἐν Κρήτῃ ταφὴν τοῦ Διὸς, τὴν ἀρχὴν τοῦ θανάτου ἱστορεῖ γεγονέναι περὶ τὸν Δία. ἀρχὴ δὲ θανάτου ἡ ἐπὶ γῆς γένεσις· λέγει δὲ οὕτως· ἐν δέ σε Παῤῥασίοις Ῥείη τέκεν εὐνηθεῖσα. ἐχρῆν δ᾿ αὐτὸν, ὡς ἠρνήσατο τὴν ἐν Κρήτῃ γένεσιν τοῦ Διὸς διὰ τὸν τάφον αὐτοῦ, ὁρᾶν ὅτι ἠκολούθει τῇ ἐν Ἀρκαδίᾳ γενέσει αὐτοῦ τὸ καὶ ἀποθανεῖν τὸν γεγεννημένον. τοιαῦτα δὲ καὶ περὶ τούτων λέγει ὁ Καλλίμαχος· Ζεῦ. σὲ μὲν Ἰδαίοισιν ἐν οὔρεσί φασι γενέσθαι, Ζεῦ, σὲ δ᾿ ἐν Ἀρκαδίῃ· πότεροι, πάτερ, ἐψεύσαντο; Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται· καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. εἰς ταῦτα δ᾿ ἡμᾶς ἤγαγεν ὁ Κέλσος. ἀγνωμονῶν περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ συγκατατιθέμενος μὲν τοῖς γεγραμμένοις, ὅτι ἀπέθανε καὶ ἐτάφη, πλάσμα δ᾿ ἡγούμενος εἶναι ὅτι καὶ ἀνέστη ἀπὸ τῶν νεκρῶν, καὶ ταῦτα μυρίων προφητῶν καὶ τοῦτο προειρηκότων καὶ πολλῶν ὄντων σημείων τῆς μετὰ θάνατον ἐπιφανείας αὐτοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: After these [things] he says (λέγω) about us that we laugh down (καταγελάω) those worshipping (προσκυνέω) Zeus, since his tomb (τάφος) is shown (δείκνυμι) in Crete, and nothing less (οὐδὲν ἧττον) we revere (σέβω) the [one] from the tomb, not knowing (οἶδα) how and in what way (καθό) Cretans do such a thing. See then that in these [words] he defends (ἀπολογέομαι) on behalf of Cretans and of Zeus and of his tomb, hinting at (αἰνίττομαι) figurative (τροπικός) underlying senses (ὑπόνοια), according to which the myth (μῦθος) about Zeus is said to have been fashioned (πλάσσω); but us he accuses (κατηγορέω), [we] agreeing (ὁμολογέω) that our Jesus was buried (θάπτω) but asserting (φάσκω) that he was also raised (ἐγείρω) from the tomb, which Cretans no longer (οὐκέτι) relate (ἱστορέω) about Zeus. Since he seems to speak in support of (συναγορεύω) the tomb of Zeus in Crete, saying ‘how and in what way Cretans do this, not knowing,’ we shall say that also the Cyrenaean Callimachus, having read very many poems (ποίημα) and having gathered up (ἀναλέγομαι) almost all Greek history (ἱστορία), knows no tropology (τροπολογία, figurative interpretation) in the [stories] about Zeus and his tomb. Therefore he also charges (ἐγκαλέω) the Cretans in the hymn (ὕμνος) written by him to Zeus, saying: ‘Cretans always liars (ψεύστης); for also a tomb, O lord (ἄναξ), of you the Cretans built (τεκταίνομαι); but you did not die (θνῄσκω), for you are always.’ And the one saying ‘you did not die, for you are always,’ having denied (ἀρνέομαι) the burial (ταφή) of Zeus in Crete, relates that the beginning (ἀρχή) of death happened concerning Zeus; and beginning of death [is] the birth (γένεσις) upon earth; he says thus: ‘and you in Parrhasia Rhea bore (τίκτω), having lain down / been bedded (εὐνάομαι).’ He ought (χρή), as he denied the Cretan birth of Zeus because of his tomb, to see that upon his birth in Arcadia followed (ἀκολουθέω) also the dying of the one born (γεννάω). Such things also about these Callimachus says: ‘Zeus, you on the Idaean mountains they say to have been born, Zeus, you in Arcadia; which (πότεροι), father, lied? Cretans always liars,’ and the next (τὰ ἑξῆς). Into these [matters] Celsus led us, being unfair (ἀγνωμονέω) about Jesus and agreeing (συγκατατίθεμαι) with the things written, that he died and was buried, but thinking (ἡγέομαι) [it] to be a fiction (πλάσμα) that he also rose (ἀνίστημι) from the dead, and this, countless (μυρίοι) prophets having also foretold (προλέγω) this, and there being many signs (σημεῖον) of his appearing (ἐπιφάνεια) after death.
pass_b_english: After this he says of us that we “laugh at those who worship Zeus, because his tomb is shown in Crete, and none the less revere the one from the tomb, not knowing how and in what sense the Cretans do such a thing.” Notice, then, that in these words he makes a defence for the Cretans, for Zeus and for his tomb, hinting at figurative meanings according to which the myth about Zeus is said to have been fashioned; but he accuses us, who admit that our Jesus was buried but declare that he was also raised from the tomb, which is something the Cretans do not go on to relate about Zeus.

Since he seems to plead for the tomb of Zeus in Crete when he says, “not knowing how and in what sense the Cretans do this,” we shall answer that even Callimachus of Cyrene, who read a vast number of poems and gathered up almost the whole of Greek history, knows of no figurative interpretation in the stories about Zeus and his tomb. That is why he reproaches the Cretans in the hymn he wrote to Zeus, saying: “Cretans are always liars; for the Cretans even built a tomb, O lord, for you; but you did not die, for you are for ever” (Callimachus, Hymn to Zeus 8–9).

Yet the man who said, “you did not die, for you are for ever,” while denying that Zeus was buried in Crete, records that the beginning of death came about for Zeus; for the beginning of death is birth upon earth. He speaks thus: “Among the Parrhasians Rhea lay down and bore you” (Callimachus, Hymn to Zeus 10). Since he denied the birth of Zeus in Crete because of his tomb, he ought to have seen that from his birth in Arcadia it followed that the one who had been born should also die. Callimachus also says this about these matters: “Zeus, some say you were born on the mountains of Ida; Zeus, others say in Arcadia. Which of them, father, have lied? Cretans are always liars” (Callimachus, Hymn to Zeus 6–8), and so on.

Celsus has led us into these matters by his unfairness about Jesus. He agrees with what is written, that he died and was buried, but he regards it as a fiction that he also rose from the dead, and this although countless prophets foretold this too, and there are many signs of his appearing after death.

choices.choice: Celsus's words are reported in indirect speech with first-person-plural verbs (καταγελῶμεν, σέβομεν, εἰδότες), so the quotation marks begin after ‘we’; the participle εἰδότες agrees with ‘we’ (the Christians), not with the Cretans. τὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ τάφου rendered literally as ‘the one from the tomb’. ὅπερ Κρῆτες οὐκέτι περὶ τοῦ Διὸς ἱστοροῦσιν: οὐκέτι taken as ‘do not go on to relate’ (the Cretans tell of a tomb but stop short of a rising). Callimachus, Hymn 1 (To Zeus): the line ‘Cretans are always liars … you are for ever’ is lines 8–9 and ‘Zeus, some say … which of them, father, have lied?’ is lines 6–7, after which Origen repeats the opening of line 8; the Rhea line is line 10. Origen's text of that line has Παῤῥασίοις … εὐνηθεῖσα; I translated the staged Greek as it stands (‘lay down’, a neutral rendering of εὐνηθεῖσα, which can also mean ‘was bedded’) and did not check it against a modern text of Callimachus. ‘Cretans are always liars’ is also quoted, from Epimenides, at Titus 1:12; Origen is quoting Callimachus here and makes no reference to Titus, so no Scripture citation is given. ‘that he died and was buried … rose from the dead’ refers to the Gospel accounts in general; the wording is close to 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, but Origen points to no single passage, so it is left uncited as a possible echo. ‘father’ for Zeus is lowercase (pagan god). μυρίων προφητῶν kept as Origen's hyperbole ‘countless prophets’. Reviewer: Origen's staged text has Παῤῥασίοις (dative plural, ‘among the Parrhasians’), where modern texts of Callimachus line 10 read Παρρασίῃ (‘in Parrhasia’); the English now follows the staged Greek.
